Hi. Thank you for seeing me. Well... I guess it’s a few things, honestly, but what finally pushed me to actually make the appointment and come in today—after staring at the clinic's phone number on my kitchen counter for at least three weeks—is that my eating has just been completely all over the place.

I’ll just push it around my plate, and my stomach feels completely closed off to the very idea of food. I just have absolutely zero interest in it. But then, it's like a switch flips, and other nights I get into this weird state where I'm just standing in the middle of the kitchen, long after everyone else has gone to bed and the house is totally quiet, and I'm just eating crackers and whatever sweets I can get my hands on. Like, just standing there in the dark by the pantry, eating saltines or graham crackers or chocolate chips right out of the bag. It's just so erratic, going from completely ignoring food to just standing there chewing in the quiet, and it's been throwing my whole life off, and I just couldn't keep ignoring it anymore, you know? Because usually I'm fairly normal about my meals, but lately it's just one extreme to the other, and it really started to worry me.

Oh, gosh, no. No, I've never done that. I know some people do, you know, to get rid of the calories or the guilt or whatever, but honestly, I absolutely hate throwing up. Well... I mean, I guess it depends on what you consider unusually large, you know? Like, if you were to compare it to a normal dinner, maybe not? But for a snack in the middle of the night, it definitely feels like a lot. So it's not like I'm eating a whole pizza or an entire cake or anything like that. It's just a bunch of random things, mostly dry stuff, honestly. But it's the fact that I just keep going back for another handful, or another cracker, until I realize I've actually eaten quite a bit of food. And it's so strange because I wasn't even hungry when I went into the kitchen. I just kind of drifted in there, and before I know it, I've eaten all these empty calories. So, I wouldn't say it's like a massive feast, but it's definitely more than I should be eating, especially when I'm just standing there in my pajamas in the dark. Well, no, not really. I don't deliberately skip meals, no. It's more like... well, because I've eaten all those crackers and chocolate chips at two in the morning, when I finally do wake up for the day—which is usually pretty late because, like I said, it takes me hours to fall back asleep after all that—I just genuinely have absolutely no appetite. 

It's not that I wake up and think, "Okay, I ate too much last night, so I'm going to punish myself by not eating breakfast." It's more that the thought of food just makes me feel slightly nauseous. My stomach still feels like it's trying to process all that dry, heavy stuff from the night before, and the heartburn is usually still lingering a bit, just kind of simmering there in my chest. So I might make a cup of coffee, maybe just black or with a little splash of milk, and I'll sit with that for a long time. 

And then lunchtime rolls around, and I might still not feel hungry, or maybe I'll just have something really small, like a piece of toast or an apple, but it's not a conscious decision to fast. It's just my body telling me it doesn't want anything else right now. I don't ever set out to restrict myself to make up for it, because honestly, I've never been one of those people who can just fast all day. If I actually get hungry, I get really irritable—my sister always calls it being "hangry"—and I get these awful headaches right behind my eyes if my blood sugar drops too low. So if I'm hungry, I eat. It's just that after those nights, the hunger just isn't there for a good portion of the next day. But it's definitely not a deliberate choice to skip a meal. It's just the natural consequence of having a stomach full of graham crackers, I suppose.

No, no, I wouldn't say I lose control. It's not like that at all. I mean, I've watched those daytime talk shows where people talk about binge eating, and they describe it like they just black out and wake up surrounded by candy wrappers and empty boxes, like some outside force just took over their body and they couldn't stop it. If the phone were to ring—not that anyone is calling at two in the morning, except maybe a wrong number, which actually happened a few months ago and scared me half to death because you always assume a middle-of-the-night call means an emergency with a family member, you know? But if the phone did ring, or if I heard a loud noise outside, I could absolutely put the box of graham crackers down and walk away without a second thought. 

So I definitely have control. I could stop at any second. It's just... I just don't really want to stop right then, I guess. Or maybe I just don't think to stop until my stomach starts getting that heavy, uncomfortable feeling I was telling you about. It's more of a quiet, mindless thing, just the soothing crunching sound in the dark kitchen while the house is so still. But I'm definitely the one deciding to put the food in my mouth, every single time. There's never a moment where I feel like I physically can't stop myself. I just kind of choose to keep going until I feel done.

Oh, absolutely. Yes, I am completely awake. I know there are people who do that sleepwalking thing, or they take certain sleeping pills—my aunt actually took something years ago, I forget the name of it, but she would wake up and find she had made a whole turkey sandwich and left the mayonnaise sitting out on the counter all night, and she had absolutely no memory of doing it. But it is not like that for me at all.

Usually it starts because my mind just suddenly turns on, maybe thinking about some random errand I forgot to run, or just replaying a conversation from a week ago, and I will lay there staring at the ceiling for a while. And once I realize I am not going back to sleep anytime soon, I get out of bed. I can feel the cold floor on my bare feet as I walk down the hallway, and I purposely do not turn on the big overhead lights because they are just too harsh and blinding at that hour, you know? I just use the little light over the stove, or the light from the inside of the refrigerator when I open the door. 

But my eyes are wide open, and my brain is fully functioning, or at least as much as it can be at two or three in the morning. I know exactly what I am doing. I remember opening the pantry, I remember specifically choosing the saltines instead of the Ritz crackers, I remember the exact sound the plastic sleeve makes when I crinkle it down to get to the next cracker. There is never any kind of trance or sleepwalking involved. I am one hundred percent conscious and aware of every single thing I am doing, which I suppose is why I remember eating it all so clearly the next morning when that heavy feeling sets in. So yes, definitely fully awake the entire time.

Because usually I'm fairly normal about my meals, but lately it's just one extreme to the other, and it really started to worry me.\n\nDoctor: After you eat like that, do you ever make yourself vomit?\n\nPatient: Oh, gosh, no. I mean, even when I actually have a stomach bug—which I had last year, right around Thanksgiving, and it was just miserable—I will fight it to the bitter end. I just completely despise the feeling of being sick like that. \n\nSo, no, after I do that... after I stand there and eat all those crackers and sweets in the dark, I just go back to bed. And I just lie there in the quiet. Sometimes I even get terrible heartburn, which I never used to get when I was younger, like in my twenties or thirties I could eat anything, but now if I eat that late, it's just this awful burning sensation in my chest. I just kind of suffer through the physical discomfort and the frustration of it all until I finally manage to drift off, which usually takes hours because I just keep turning it over in my head. I don't really know. Well, I definitely stay awake. Like I said, once I'm up, my mind is just racing, and the eating is something I do while I'm fully, completely awake. I'll just stand there in the kitchen, and it's so quiet—you can hear the refrigerator humming, which always sounds so loud at 2 AM—and I'll eat, say, half a sleeve of saltines. And then I think, well, I want something sweet now, so I'll grab a handful of chocolate chips. And then maybe another handful. And then I'll find a box of graham crackers and eat three or four sheets of those. \n\nSo it's not like I'm eating a whole pizza or an entire cake or anything like that. It's just a bunch of random things, mostly dry stuff, honestly. But it's the fact that I just keep going back for another handful, or another cracker, until I realize I've actually eaten quite a bit of food. And it's so strange because I wasn't even hungry when I went into the kitchen. I just kind of drifted in there, and before I know it, I've eaten all these empty calories. So, I wouldn't say it's like a massive feast, but it's definitely more than I should be eating, especially when I'm just standing there in my pajamas in the dark. It just feels like a lot because of how heavy it sits in my stomach afterward, you know? Like I said, the heartburn is just awful, and it makes me realize that, wow, I really did just eat a lot of crackers. But is it an unusually large amount compared to someone else? I don't really know. I just know it feels like too much for me, at that time of night.\n\nDoctor: After those nighttime eating episodes, do you ever deliberately skip meals or fast the next day to make up for it?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I don't deliberately skip meals, no. It's more like... well, because I've eaten all those crackers and chocolate chips at two in the morning, when I finally do wake up for the day—which is usually pretty late because, like I said, it takes me hours to fall back asleep after all that—I just genuinely have absolutely no appetite. \n\nIt's not that I wake up and think, \"Okay, I ate too much last night, so I'm going to punish myself by not eating breakfast.\" It's more that the thought of food just makes me feel slightly nauseous. My stomach still feels like it's trying to process all that dry, heavy stuff from the night before, and the heartburn is usually still lingering a bit, just kind of simmering there in my chest. So I might make a cup of coffee, maybe just black or with a little splash of milk, and I'll sit with that for a long time. \n\nAnd then lunchtime rolls around, and I might still not feel hungry, or maybe I'll just have something really small, like a piece of toast or an apple, but it's not a conscious decision to fast. It's just my body telling me it doesn't want anything else right now. I don't ever set out to restrict myself to make up for it, because honestly, I've never been one of those people who can just fast all day. If I actually get hungry, I get really irritable—my sister always calls it being \"hangry\"—and I get these awful headaches right behind my eyes if my blood sugar drops too low. So if I'm hungry, I eat. It's just that after those nights, the hunger just isn't there for a good portion of the next day. But it's definitely not a deliberate choice to skip a meal. It's just the natural consequence of having a stomach full of graham crackers, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: When these nighttime eating episodes happen, do you feel like you lose control and can’t stop eating once you start?\n\nPatient: No, no, I wouldn't say I lose control. It's not like that at all. I mean, I've watched those daytime talk shows where people talk about binge eating, and they describe it like they just black out and wake up surrounded by candy wrappers and empty boxes, like some outside force just took over their body and they couldn't stop it. It's definitely not like that for me. I'm fully aware that I'm standing there in the kitchen eating. \n\nI'll eat a saltine, and I'll think, well, that was salty, now I want a chocolate chip. And I make the conscious choice to reach into the bag. If the phone were to ring—not that anyone is calling at two in the morning, except maybe a wrong number, which actually happened a few months ago and scared me half to death because you always assume a middle-of-the-night call means an emergency with a family member, you know? But if the phone did ring, or if I heard a loud noise outside, I could absolutely put the box of graham crackers down and walk away without a second thought. \n\nSo I definitely have control. I could stop at any second. It's just... I just don't really want to stop right then, I guess. Or maybe I just don't think to stop until my stomach starts getting that heavy, uncomfortable feeling I was telling you about. It's more of a quiet, mindless thing, just the soothing crunching sound in the dark kitchen while the house is so still. But I'm definitely the one deciding to put the food in my mouth, every single time. There's never a moment where I feel like I physically can't stop myself. I just kind of choose to keep going until I feel done.\n\nDoctor: When you get up and eat in the middle of the night, are you fully awake and aware the whole time?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. And once I realize I am not going back to sleep anytime soon, I get out of bed. I can feel the cold floor on my bare feet as I walk down the hallway, and I purposely do not turn on the big overhead lights because they are just too harsh and blinding at that hour, you know? I just use the little light over the stove, or the light from the inside of the refrigerator when I open the door. \n\nBut my eyes are wide open, and my brain is fully functioning, or at least as much as it can be at two or three in the morning. I know exactly what I am doing. There is never any kind of trance or sleepwalking involved. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
No, no, it’s not about losing weight. I mean, I see all those magazines at the grocery checkout, you know, the ones promising you can lose ten pounds in a week if you just drink cabbage soup or only eat between noon and six p.m. or whatever the new trend is. And I have friends who are constantly counting calories or points or macros—whatever those are—and they’ll sit at lunch and agonize over whether to have the salad dressing on the side. But I don't do any of that. I'm really not trying to diet or restrict myself on purpose. 

Like I was saying before about the roast chicken, when I don't eat during the day, it has absolutely nothing to do with wanting to be thinner or trying to fit into a certain pair of jeans. I've been pretty much the exact same size for years now, give or take a little bit around the holidays, which I think is pretty normal for anyone. But when I'm sitting there staring at my plate, it’s not a conscious choice to restrict my food. It’s just... the desire is completely gone. It's like my brain just disconnects from my stomach. If I were actually trying to lose weight, I definitely wouldn't be standing in the kitchen at three in the morning eating handfuls of chocolate chips and graham crackers, right? That would completely defeat the whole purpose of a diet! 

So, no, I’m never skipping lunch because I want to drop a dress size. If I don't eat, it's just because the actual physical act of picking up the fork, chewing, and swallowing just feels so... exhausting. Like it’s just too much effort and I have absolutely zero interest in it. I actually really wish I could just eat a normal lunch and a normal dinner like a regular person, because maybe then my stomach wouldn't be so empty and confused in the middle of the night. But no, it's definitely not any sort of intentional weight loss thing.

It's just my body telling me it doesn't want anything else right now. I don't ever set out to restrict myself to make up for it, because honestly, I've never been one of those people who can just fast all day. Well, I don't know if I'd call it a binge, really. And then I'll find a box of graham crackers and eat three or four sheets of those. \n\nSo it's not like I'm eating a whole pizza or an entire cake or anything like that. It's just a bunch of random things, mostly dry stuff, honestly. But it's the fact that I just keep going back for another handful, or another cracker, until I realize I've actually eaten quite a bit of food. And it's so strange because I wasn't even hungry when I went into the kitchen. I just kind of drifted in there, and before I know it, I've eaten all these empty calories. So, I wouldn't say it's like a massive feast, but it's definitely more than I should be eating, especially when I'm just standing there in my pajamas in the dark. It just feels like a lot because of how heavy it sits in my stomach afterward, you know? Like I said, the heartburn is just awful, and it makes me realize that, wow, I really did just eat a lot of crackers. But is it an unusually large amount compared to someone else? I don't really know. I just know it feels like too much for me, at that time of night.\n\nDoctor: After those nighttime eating episodes, do you ever deliberately skip meals or fast the next day to make up for it?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I don't deliberately skip meals, no. It's more like... well, because I've eaten all those crackers and chocolate chips at two in the morning, when I finally do wake up for the day—which is usually pretty late because, like I said, it takes me hours to fall back asleep after all that—I just genuinely have absolutely no appetite. \n\nIt's not that I wake up and think, \"Okay, I ate too much last night, so I'm going to punish myself by not eating breakfast.\" It's more that the thought of food just makes me feel slightly nauseous. My stomach still feels like it's trying to process all that dry, heavy stuff from the night before, and the heartburn is usually still lingering a bit, just kind of simmering there in my chest. So I might make a cup of coffee, maybe just black or with a little splash of milk, and I'll sit with that for a long time. \n\nAnd then lunchtime rolls around, and I might still not feel hungry, or maybe I'll just have something really small, like a piece of toast or an apple, but it's not a conscious decision to fast. It's just my body telling me it doesn't want anything else right now. I don't ever set out to restrict myself to make up for it, because honestly, I've never been one of those people who can just fast all day. If I actually get hungry, I get really irritable—my sister always calls it being \"hangry\"—and I get these awful headaches right behind my eyes if my blood sugar drops too low. So if I'm hungry, I eat. It's just that after those nights, the hunger just isn't there for a good portion of the next day. But it's definitely not a deliberate choice to skip a meal. It's just the natural consequence of having a stomach full of graham crackers, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: When these nighttime eating episodes happen, do you feel like you lose control and can’t stop eating once you start?\n\nPatient: No, no, I wouldn't say I lose control. It's not like that at all. I mean, I've watched those daytime talk shows where people talk about binge eating, and they describe it like they just black out and wake up surrounded by candy wrappers and empty boxes, like some outside force just took over their body and they couldn't stop it. It's definitely not like that for me. I'm fully aware that I'm standing there in the kitchen eating. \n\nI'll eat a saltine, and I'll think, well, that was salty, now I want a chocolate chip. And I make the conscious choice to reach into the bag. If the phone were to ring—not that anyone is calling at two in the morning, except maybe a wrong number, which actually happened a few months ago and scared me half to death because you always assume a middle-of-the-night call means an emergency with a family member, you know? But if the phone did ring, or if I heard a loud noise outside, I could absolutely put the box of graham crackers down and walk away without a second thought. \n\nSo I definitely have control. I could stop at any second. It's just... I just don't really want to stop right then, I guess. Or maybe I just don't think to stop until my stomach starts getting that heavy, uncomfortable feeling I was telling you about. It's more of a quiet, mindless thing, just the soothing crunching sound in the dark kitchen while the house is so still. But I'm definitely the one deciding to put the food in my mouth, every single time. There's never a moment where I feel like I physically can't stop myself. I just kind of choose to keep going until I feel done.\n\nDoctor: When you get up and eat in the middle of the night, are you fully awake and aware the whole time?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Yes, I am completely awake. I know there are people who do that sleepwalking thing, or they take certain sleeping pills—my aunt actually took something years ago, I forget the name of it, but she would wake up and find she had made a whole turkey sandwich and left the mayonnaise sitting out on the counter all night, and she had absolutely no memory of doing it. But it is not like that for me at all. \n\nWhen I wake up, I am very much awake. Usually it starts because my mind just suddenly turns on, maybe thinking about some random errand I forgot to run, or just replaying a conversation from a week ago, and I will lay there staring at the ceiling for a while. And once I realize I am not going back to sleep anytime soon, I get out of bed. I can feel the cold floor on my bare feet as I walk down the hallway, and I purposely do not turn on the big overhead lights because they are just too harsh and blinding at that hour, you know? I just use the little light over the stove, or the light from the inside of the refrigerator when I open the door. \n\nBut my eyes are wide open, and my brain is fully functioning, or at least as much as it can be at two or three in the morning. I know exactly what I am doing. I remember opening the pantry, I remember specifically choosing the saltines instead of the Ritz crackers, I remember the exact sound the plastic sleeve makes when I crinkle it down to get to the next cracker. There is never any kind of trance or sleepwalking involved. I am one hundred percent conscious and aware of every single thing I am doing, which I suppose is why I remember eating it all so clearly the next morning when that heavy feeling sets in. So yes, definitely fully awake the entire time.\n\nDoctor: When you wake up in the middle of the night to eat, do you ever eat and then go back to sleep while still half-asleep, or do you stay awake afterward?\n\nPatient: Well, I definitely stay awake. It's just been so all over the place lately, and it's starting to really bother me. \n\nSome weeks, I just have absolutely zero interest in food. I'll make a nice dinner, maybe a roast chicken with those little red potatoes that I usually love, and I'll sit down at the table and just... stare at it. I'll barely touch a thing, maybe push a carrot around my plate so it looks like I ate, but I just can't bring myself to swallow it. And then, just when I think I'm never going to eat a normal meal again, I have those nights where I'm standing in the dark kitchen after everyone else has gone to bed, just eating handful after handful of crackers and chocolate chips, completely wide awake. \n\nAnd after I eat all that, I definitely don't just drift back to sleep. Oh, no. I'll go back to bed, sure, but I'll just lie there. My stomach will be doing flips from all the sugar and dry crackers, and my brain will just be going a mile a minute. I might toss and turn for another two or three hours before I even get close to dozing off again. So, no, there's no half-asleep eating and going right back to bed for me. I'm awake for the eating, and I'm awake for a long time after, just dealing with the aftermath of it all. It's exhausting, really, this constant back-and-forth between not eating at all and then doing... whatever it is I'm doing in the middle of the night.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever intentionally try to lose weight by restricting how much you eat during the day?\n\nPatient: No, no, it’s not about losing weight. I mean, I see all those magazines at the grocery checkout, you know, the ones promising you can lose ten pounds in a week if you just drink cabbage soup or only eat between noon and six p.m. or whatever the new trend is. But no, it's definitely not any sort of intentional weight loss thing.\n\nDoctor: When you have these nighttime eating episodes, would you say you eat a truly large amount of food, like enough that most other people would consider it a binge?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't know if I'd call it a binge, really. Well, like I was just saying, I really wouldn't consider it an objectively large amount of food. I mean, it's not like I'm emptying out the refrigerator or anything dramatic like that. I'm not sitting there eating an entire loaf of bread or a whole box of cereal in one go. It's really just... bits and pieces, you know? A handful of this, a slice of that. 

Like last Tuesday, or maybe it was Wednesday—no, it was Tuesday because it was raining—I got up and I had maybe five or six crackers, and then I found an apple in the crisper drawer, so I sliced that up, and then I had a little piece of cheddar cheese to go with it. And then, because the cheese was a bit sharp, I wanted something sweet, so I had a few of those chocolate chips I keep in the baking cabinet. But if you put it all on a plate together, it wouldn't even look like a full meal. It certainly wouldn't look like an objectively large amount of food to anyone else. It's just that it feels like a lot to me because it's three in the morning and the house is dead quiet and I know I shouldn't be eating at all. 

So, no, if someone were to measure it out or look at it objectively, they wouldn't say, "My goodness, she's eating a massive amount." It's just the grazing, the constant back-and-forth between the pantry and the fridge for an hour or so while my mind is racing. Well, I don't know if "unable to stop" is exactly the right way to put it. I mean, it's not like I'm completely out of control, like some sort of machine that just keeps eating until it breaks, you know? It's more like... I just don't want to stop. Or maybe I feel like I *can't* stop until I've found exactly the right combination of things. 

Like, I'll start with the crackers, and then I'll think, "Oh, maybe I need something a little salty," so I'll grab a pickle from the jar in the back of the fridge—the dill ones, not the sweet ones, I can't stand the sweet ones—and then the pickle makes me want something to drink, so I'll pour a small glass of milk, and then the milk makes me think of cookies, even if I don't have any cookies, so I'll go looking for something sweet again. 

It's this whole chain reaction. And while I'm doing it, part of my brain is saying, "You should probably go back to bed now, it's 3:30 in the morning," but the other part is just so focused on the next bite, the next flavor. It's almost like a trance, standing there in the kitchen light. I guess I could physically force myself to walk away and shut the pantry door, but in the moment, it just feels like I have to finish the cycle. I have to graze until I feel satisfied, or until the quiet in the house stops feeling so loud, if that makes any sense. So, I wouldn't say I'm completely unable to stop, but it certainly feels very, very difficult to just cut it off once I've started that whole routine.

Well, that's actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and see you, because my eating has just been completely all over the place lately. It's so unpredictable. I mean, yes, to answer your question, a lot of it does happen late at night, but it's not a consistent thing where I eat a normal dinner and then just snack later. It's more like... some weeks, I'll make a whole dinner—like a nice roast or a casserole, something I usually love—and I'll just sit there pushing it around my plate. I barely touch it. My husband will ask if I'm feeling okay, and I just have zero appetite for a proper evening meal. It just seems like too much effort to chew and swallow, you know?

But then, on other nights, or even during those same weeks where I skip dinner, I'll wake up at two or three in the morning, and suddenly I'm standing in the kitchen in the dark. After everyone else has gone to bed and the whole house is asleep, there I am, eating crackers and sweets and whatever else I can find. It's like my body doesn't know when it's supposed to be hungry anymore. It’s completely backwards. I’ll have practically nothing at 6:00 PM, and then at 3:00 AM I'm scrounging through the pantry for chocolate chips and cheese. So, yes, a huge portion of what I actually do eat ends up being late at night, but it's part of this whole frustrating pattern where my appetite just completely disappears during normal meal times and then ambushes me when I should be sleeping. I just use the little light over the stove, or the light from the inside of the refrigerator when I open the door. \n\nBut my eyes are wide open, and my brain is fully functioning, or at least as much as it can be at two or three in the morning. I know exactly what I am doing. I remember opening the pantry, I remember specifically choosing the saltines instead of the Ritz crackers, I remember the exact sound the plastic sleeve makes when I crinkle it down to get to the next cracker. There is never any kind of trance or sleepwalking involved. I am one hundred percent conscious and aware of every single thing I am doing, which I suppose is why I remember eating it all so clearly the next morning when that heavy feeling sets in. So yes, definitely fully awake the entire time.\n\nDoctor: When you wake up in the middle of the night to eat, do you ever eat and then go back to sleep while still half-asleep, or do you stay awake afterward?\n\nPatient: Well, I definitely stay awake. It's just been so all over the place lately, and it's starting to really bother me. \n\nSome weeks, I just have absolutely zero interest in food. I'll make a nice dinner, maybe a roast chicken with those little red potatoes that I usually love, and I'll sit down at the table and just... stare at it. I'll barely touch a thing, maybe push a carrot around my plate so it looks like I ate, but I just can't bring myself to swallow it. And then, just when I think I'm never going to eat a normal meal again, I have those nights where I'm standing in the dark kitchen after everyone else has gone to bed, just eating handful after handful of crackers and chocolate chips, completely wide awake. \n\nAnd after I eat all that, I definitely don't just drift back to sleep. Oh, no. I'll go back to bed, sure, but I'll just lie there. My stomach will be doing flips from all the sugar and dry crackers, and my brain will just be going a mile a minute. I might toss and turn for another two or three hours before I even get close to dozing off again. So, no, there's no half-asleep eating and going right back to bed for me. I'm awake for the eating, and I'm awake for a long time after, just dealing with the aftermath of it all. It's exhausting, really, this constant back-and-forth between not eating at all and then doing... whatever it is I'm doing in the middle of the night.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever intentionally try to lose weight by restricting how much you eat during the day?\n\nPatient: No, no, it’s not about losing weight. I mean, I see all those magazines at the grocery checkout, you know, the ones promising you can lose ten pounds in a week if you just drink cabbage soup or only eat between noon and six p.m. or whatever the new trend is. Well, if I really sit down and trace it back, I'd say it's been happening for about two years and five months now. I know that sounds oddly specific, but I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time things at home got really... intense.

Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't call it a massive amount of food, not like those people you see on TV who eat, you know, five pizzas in one sitting. It's not like that at all. It's more about the... the specific things I choose and the ritual of it, I guess. 

Like, I'll go in there, and the house is completely silent, right? The only sound is the hum of the refrigerator. And I'll open the door, and the light is so bright it almost hurts my eyes after being in the dark hallway. I'll stand there, and I'll pull out... well, let's say I pull out a sleeve of saltine crackers and a jar of peanut butter. I won't eat the whole sleeve, and I won't eat the whole jar. I'll maybe have six or seven crackers, but I'll spread the peanut butter perfectly, edge to edge, making sure it's completely even. And maybe I'll have a few slices of turkey deli meat—not the whole package, just three or four slices, and I have to roll them up tightly before I eat them. 

Then I might move on to something sweet, but again, it's not a whole cake. It might be a handful of chocolate chips from the baking pantry, the semi-sweet ones, not the milk chocolate, and I'll eat them one by one, letting each one melt on my tongue before I have the next. It's very methodical. It takes time. I might be standing in the kitchen for forty-five minutes or an hour, just sort of grazing, moving from the crackers to the turkey to the chocolate chips, and maybe pouring a small glass of milk, but only filling it halfway. 

So when you ask if it's a "very large amount in a short period," the answer is really no. It's actually quite a small to moderate amount of food, but it's stretched out over this long, quiet period where I'm just trying to soothe myself, trying to quiet down all the buzzing in my head about the art projects and the arguments with my husband. It's the act of eating, the textures, the quietness of the house—that's what it's about, not stuffing myself with thousands of calories in ten minutes. I'm very aware of what I'm eating, like I said before, and I'm not gorging myself. It's just... it's just a slow, quiet escape, really.

And I have friends who are constantly counting calories or points or macros—whatever those are—and they’ll sit at lunch and agonize over whether to have the salad dressing on the side. No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's never a feeling of being out of control or being unable to stop. Like I was trying to explain before, I know exactly what I'm doing every second I'm down there. If I wanted to stop, I could stop at any moment. And the moment that thought clicked into place, I just... put the cheese down. I didn't even eat it. I wrapped the block back up in the plastic wrap, very carefully making sure no air could get in so the edges wouldn't dry out, put it back in the deli drawer, washed the knife, dried it with the blue towel, and walked right back upstairs. 

So, there's absolutely no compulsion driving me where I feel like my hands are moving on their own or something. I'm very present. It's more like I'm choosing to be there because it's the only place that feels grounded when my mind is just buzzing with all these concepts and connections. I eat because I want to, because the crunch of a cracker or the coldness of a glass of milk is something real and tangible I can focus on. But if I hear my husband shift in bed upstairs, or if I suddenly figure out a solution to an art problem, I just stop. I close the fridge, I wipe the counter so there are no crumbs left behind, and I'm done. I never feel trapped by the eating. It's not like a runaway train at all. It's more like a... a gentle stroll that I can end whenever I feel like I've walked far enough. I know some people probably struggle with that, where they just can't stop themselves once they start, but for me, the stopping is just as deliberate and controlled as the starting. I'm always the one in the driver's seat with it.

If I were actually trying to lose weight, I definitely wouldn't be standing in the kitchen at three in the morning eating handfuls of chocolate chips and graham crackers, right? That would completely defeat the whole purpose of a diet! \n\nSo, no, I’m never skipping lunch because I want to drop a dress size. If I don't eat, it's just because the actual physical act of picking up the fork, chewing, and swallowing just feels so... exhausting. Like it’s just too much effort and I have absolutely zero interest in it. I actually really wish I could just eat a normal lunch and a normal dinner like a regular person, because maybe then my stomach wouldn't be so empty and confused in the middle of the night. But no, it's definitely not any sort of intentional weight loss thing.\n\nDoctor: When you have these nighttime eating episodes, would you say you eat a truly large amount of food, like enough that most other people would consider it a binge?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't know if I'd call it a binge, really. I mean, when I hear the word binge, I think of someone sitting down and eating, like, three whole pizzas and a gallon of ice cream in one sitting, you know? Like on those television shows where people are hiding food wrappers under their bed. It's not like that. It's just... a lot of snacking, I guess? \n\nLike I said, it might be a sleeve of saltines, or a handful of chocolate chips, maybe some graham crackers. Sometimes I'll make a piece of toast, and then while I'm eating the toast, I'll have a few slices of cheese straight from the deli bag. But it's not like I'm cooking a second dinner or eating a mountain of food that would shock anyone. It's more just... continuous grazing while I'm standing there in the quiet. I don't think it's a massive amount of food, not like what you'd see in a movie or something. It just feels like a lot to me because it's the middle of the night and my stomach is usually so empty from not eating during the day. But I don't think other people would look at it and say, \"Wow, that's a crazy amount of food.\" It's just the timing of it all that's so frustrating, and the fact that I just can't seem to stop myself from opening the pantry once I'm up.\n\nDoctor: When you have these nighttime eating episodes, do you ever eat an objectively large amount of food in one sitting?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying, I really wouldn't consider it an objectively large amount of food. I mean, it's not like I'm emptying out the refrigerator or anything dramatic like that. I'm not sitting there eating an entire loaf of bread or a whole box of cereal in one go. It's really just... bits and pieces, you know? A handful of this, a slice of that. \n\nLike last Tuesday, or maybe it was Wednesday—no, it was Tuesday because it was raining—I got up and I had maybe five or six crackers, and then I found an apple in the crisper drawer, so I sliced that up, and then I had a little piece of cheddar cheese to go with it. And then, because the cheese was a bit sharp, I wanted something sweet, so I had a few of those chocolate chips I keep in the baking cabinet. But if you put it all on a plate together, it wouldn't even look like a full meal. It certainly wouldn't look like an objectively large amount of food to anyone else. It's just that it feels like a lot to me because it's three in the morning and the house is dead quiet and I know I shouldn't be eating at all. \n\nSo, no, if someone were to measure it out or look at it objectively, they wouldn't say, \"My goodness, she's eating a massive amount.\" It's just the grazing, the constant back-and-forth between the pantry and the fridge for an hour or so while my mind is racing. It's the habit of it, the timing, not the actual sheer volume of the food itself. I really don't think it's enough food to be considered objectively large by any stretch of the imagination.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling depressed or down most days lately?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I do. I mean, not every single second of every single day, but I definitely go through these... these stretches, I guess you'd call them. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like the whole house just feels gray and heavy, you know? Like the air itself is thick and it takes effort just to walk from the bedroom to the living room. \n\nI’ll just sit there at the kitchen table—the one by the window where the sun usually comes in during the morning, though lately even the sun doesn't seem to make much of a difference—and I just feel so completely empty. And the strange thing is, it’s not like anything terrible has happened. It’s not like I got bad news or got into an argument with anyone or watched a sad movie. It’s just this overwhelming sense of... nothingness. It just settles over me like a heavy blanket. \n\nAnd it lasts for days, sometimes weeks, where I just can't shake that heavy feeling. I’ll look around at the mail piling up on the counter, or the dishes I haven't washed, and I know I should care, I know I should just get up and do something, but I just sit there staring at the grain of the wood on the table. It’s like all the color has just drained right out of my life, and I can't figure out how to get it back. So, yes, I guess you could say I've been feeling pretty down. It's just so exhausting feeling that heavy all the time when there's no real reason for it.\n\nDoctor: When these nighttime eating episodes happen, do you feel unable to stop eating once you start?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't know if \"unable to stop\" is exactly the right way to put it. I mean, it's not like I'm completely out of control, like some sort of machine that just keeps eating until it breaks, you know? It's more like... I just don't want to stop. Or maybe I feel like I *can't* stop until I've found exactly the right combination of things. \n\nLike, I'll start with the crackers, and then I'll think, \"Oh, maybe I need something a little salty,\" so I'll grab a pickle from the jar in the back of the fridge—the dill ones, not the sweet ones, I can't stand the sweet ones—and then the pickle makes me want something to drink, so I'll pour a small glass of milk, and then the milk makes me think of cookies, even if I don't have any cookies, so I'll go looking for something sweet again. \n\nIt's this whole chain reaction. And while I'm doing it, part of my brain is saying, \"You should probably go back to bed now, it's 3:30 in the morning,\" but the other part is just so focused on the next bite, the next flavor. It's almost like a trance, standing there in the kitchen light. I guess I could physically force myself to walk away and shut the pantry door, but in the moment, it just feels like I have to finish the cycle. I have to graze until I feel satisfied, or until the quiet in the house stops feeling so loud, if that makes any sense. So, I wouldn't say I'm completely unable to stop, but it certainly feels very, very difficult to just cut it off once I've started that whole routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that most of your food intake happens after your evening meal or later at night?\n\nPatient: Well, that's actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and see you, because my eating has just been completely all over the place lately. It's so unpredictable. I mean, yes, to answer your question, a lot of it does happen late at night, but it's not a consistent thing where I eat a normal dinner and then just snack later. It's more like... some weeks, I'll make a whole dinner—like a nice roast or a casserole, something I usually love—and I'll just sit there pushing it around my plate. I barely touch it. My husband will ask if I'm feeling okay, and I just have zero appetite for a proper evening meal. It just seems like too much effort to chew and swallow, you know?\n\nBut then, on other nights, or even during those same weeks where I skip dinner, I'll wake up at two or three in the morning, and suddenly I'm standing in the kitchen in the dark. After everyone else has gone to bed and the whole house is asleep, there I am, eating crackers and sweets and whatever else I can find. It's like my body doesn't know when it's supposed to be hungry anymore. It’s completely backwards. I’ll have practically nothing at 6:00 PM, and then at 3:00 AM I'm scrounging through the pantry for chocolate chips and cheese. So, yes, a huge portion of what I actually do eat ends up being late at night, but it's part of this whole frustrating pattern where my appetite just completely disappears during normal meal times and then ambushes me when I should be sleeping. It's just been driving me crazy trying to make sense of it.\n\nDoctor: When you get up to eat at night, has anyone ever seen you do it while you were still asleep?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not that I know of. I mean, my husband is a very heavy sleeper, so once he's out, he's out for the night. You could probably drive a truck through the living room and he wouldn't even stir. But as for me, I'm definitely awake when I do it. I mean, I remember everything. \n\nIt's not like sleepwalking, where you wake up the next morning and find a half-eaten sandwich on the counter and wonder who made it. I know exactly what I'm doing. I remember getting out of bed, feeling the cold floor on my feet, walking down the hallway, trying to avoid that one floorboard right outside the bathroom that always creaks because I don't want to wake anyone up. I remember opening the pantry, looking at the shelves, deciding between the saltines or the graham crackers. \n\nI'm completely conscious the whole time. Sometimes I even stand there and argue with myself about it in my head, thinking, \"You really don't need to be eating this right now,\" but I just do it anyway. And then I remember going back to bed, brushing the crumbs off my hands, and trying to get comfortable again. So, no, nobody has ever caught me doing it while I was asleep, because I'm definitely, one hundred percent awake when it happens. I just wish I wasn't awake, honestly. It would almost be easier to explain if I was just sleepwalking, you know? But no, I'm awake for every single bite.\n\nDoctor: How long have these nighttime eating episodes been going on?\n\nPatient: Well, if I really sit down and trace it back, I'd say it's been happening for about two years and five months now. I know that sounds oddly specific, but I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time things at home got really... intense. \n\nMy husband and I started having these massive arguments. And it wasn't just about normal things, it was about my spending, and specifically, my art projects. I had started this really elaborate mixed-media series—I was collecting all these different textures, fabrics, metals, things I found that just spoke to me, you know? I needed them because I could see the connections between all the materials, how they were supposed to fit together to reveal this bigger pattern that I felt like only I was noticing. But he didn't understand it. He just saw the credit card bills and the boxes of supplies piling up in the spare room. He called it \"junk\" and said I was wasting our money on nonsense. \n\nIt was so incredibly stressful, feeling like I was on the verge of this major creative breakthrough and having the person who is supposed to support me just completely shut it down and yell at me about receipts. The tension in the house was just suffocating. I couldn't sleep because my mind was racing with all the ideas for my art, and also just the anger from our fights. So, I'd get up. I'd wander into the kitchen just to get away from him snoring in the bed, and that's when the eating in the middle of the night began. It was like the only quiet time I had to myself where I wasn't being criticized. So yeah, two years and five months of this whole routine, right since those arguments really started escalating and making me feel like I was crawling out of my own skin.\n\nDoctor: When you eat at night, do you remember it clearly the next morning?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, I think I just mentioned that, but yes, I remember every single detail. It’s not fuzzy at all. Like I said, I'm completely awake, so the next morning, I know exactly what I ate, how much of it I ate, and even what I was thinking while I was eating it. \n\nI remember waking up, I remember the whole debate I have with myself while I'm standing in front of the open fridge, letting the cold air just spill out onto my feet. I'll be looking at, say, a block of cheddar cheese and a half-empty jar of pickles, and I'll remember thinking, \"This is a terrible combination, why are you doing this?\" but then I do it anyway. And then the next morning, when I go into the kitchen to make coffee, I'll see the knife I left in the sink or the crumbs on the counter, and it just confirms what I already know. I remember it all perfectly clearly. There’s no mystery about it, no waking up and wondering who ate the last of the crackers. It was me, and I remember every bite of it, clear as day.\n\nDoctor: Has this eating pattern been causing you significant distress or interfering with your daily life, work, or relationships?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I mean, it really has been causing a lot of problems, more than I probably wanted to admit at first. It’s not just the eating itself, it’s the whole... ripple effect of everything that’s been going on. I mean, my daily life is just completely thrown off track. \n\nFor one thing, I was doing this facilitator training program online, which I was really excited about, and I also have this private blog where I write and share things—mostly my thoughts on my art and the connections I was telling you about earlier. But I’ve fallen so far behind on all of it. I sit down at the computer, and it’s like my brain just won’t cooperate. I have all these ideas, these incredibly complex, beautiful ideas, but when I try to organize them or explain them in a way that makes sense for the blog or the training modules, it just gets so jumbled. It’s like trying to untangle a massive knot of yarn, and I just end up staring at the screen for hours, feeling completely overwhelmed. I can't seem to get the thoughts from my head into a structured format anymore. \n\nAnd then, of course, there’s my husband. The tension at home is just... it’s thick. You could cut it with a knife. Because of the arguments about my projects and the money, and then me being up half the night eating and pacing, we just don't have any sort of normal routine anymore. We hardly eat meals together, we definitely don't go to bed at the same time, and when we do cross paths in the kitchen or the hallway, it’s just this awkward, heavy silence, or it immediately turns into another disagreement. It’s exhausting. It really is. I feel like I'm letting everything slip through my fingers—my training, my writing, my marriage—and I just can't seem to find the energy or the focus to pull it all back together. So, yes, the distress is very real, and it’s definitely interfering with pretty much every part of my life right now.\n\nDoctor: During these nighttime episodes, do you ever eat what would clearly be considered a very large amount of food in a short period of time?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't call it a massive amount of food, not like those people you see on TV who eat, you know, five pizzas in one sitting. It's not like that at all. It's more about the... the specific things I choose and the ritual of it, I guess. \n\nLike, I'll go in there, and the house is completely silent, right? The only sound is the hum of the refrigerator. And I'll open the door, and the light is so bright it almost hurts my eyes after being in the dark hallway. It might be a handful of chocolate chips from the baking pantry, the semi-sweet ones, not the milk chocolate, and I'll eat them one by one, letting each one melt on my tongue before I have the next. It's very methodical. It takes time. I might be standing in the kitchen for forty-five minutes or an hour, just sort of grazing, moving from the crackers to the turkey to the chocolate chips, and maybe pouring a small glass of milk, but only filling it halfway. \n\nSo when you ask if it's a \"very large amount in a short period,\" the answer is really no. It's actually quite a small to moderate amount of food, but it's stretched out over this long, quiet period where I'm just trying to soothe myself, trying to quiet down all the buzzing in my head about the art projects and the arguments with my husband. It's the act of eating, the textures, the quietness of the house—that's what it's about, not stuffing myself with thousands of calories in ten minutes. I'm very aware of what I'm eating, like I said before, and I'm not gorging myself. It's just... it's just a slow, quiet escape, really.\n\nDoctor: During those nighttime eating episodes, would you say you consume a clearly large amount of food in a short period of time, like an objectively big binge?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, I think I just went over this, but no, definitely not. It's not a binge, not at all. When I hear \"binge,\" I think of someone just completely out of control, shoving food in their mouth as fast as they can, not even tasting it, just... consuming. That is absolutely not what I do. \n\nLike I was saying, it's very slow. It's almost... well, it's very deliberate. I'm not eating a whole carton of ice cream or ordering three pizzas. It's really just a few things here and there. A couple of crackers, maybe some cheese, a handful of grapes if we have them. I'll take a bite, chew it slowly, look out the window at the streetlights, think about whatever it is that woke me up in the first place... usually it's the art, the connections I was telling you about, how the colors need to flow together. It's drawn out. It's pacing around the kitchen island, opening the pantry, looking at the cans, deciding I don't want soup, closing the pantry, opening the fridge again. I might be down there for an hour and a half and only eat, you know, the equivalent of a small sandwich and a few chips. It's not about volume. It's really not. It's about the quiet, the routine of it, having something to do with my hands and my mouth while my brain is just spinning and spinning. So to call it an \"objectively big binge\" just doesn't fit the reality of what's happening at all. It's a very small amount of food, really, when you look at how long I'm actually awake and down there in the kitchen.\n\nDoctor: During those nighttime eating episodes, do you ever feel like you’re unable to stop eating even if you want to?\n\nPatient: No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's never a feeling of being out of control or being unable to stop. Like I was trying to explain before, I know exactly what I'm doing every second I'm down there. If I wanted to stop, I could stop at any moment. In fact, sometimes I do stop right in the middle of preparing something. \n\nLike just the other night—I think it was Tuesday, or maybe Wednesday because it was raining and the sound of the rain against the kitchen window was actually really soothing—anyway, I was standing there with a block of sharp cheddar cheese. I had the little paring knife with the black handle, the one we keep in the secondary drawer, and I had just sliced off this perfectly even, thin square of cheese. I was just about to take a bite, but then I had this sudden, very clear thought about the canvas I'd been working on in the spare room. The one with the heavy, textured yellow strokes that I was telling you about. I suddenly realized how I needed to balance the yellow with a specific wash of indigo. \n\nAnd the moment that thought clicked into place, I just... put the cheese down. I didn't even eat it. I wrapped the block back up in the plastic wrap, very carefully making sure no air could get in so the edges wouldn't dry out, put it back in the deli drawer, washed the knife, dried it with the blue towel, and walked right back upstairs. \n\nSo, there's absolutely no compulsion driving me where I feel like my hands are moving on their own or something. I'm very present. It's more like I'm choosing to be there because it's the only place that feels grounded when my mind is just buzzing with all these concepts and connections. I eat because I want to, because the crunch of a cracker or the coldness of a glass of milk is something real and tangible I can focus on. But if I hear my husband shift in bed upstairs, or if I suddenly figure out a solution to an art problem, I just stop. I close the fridge, I wipe the counter so there are no crumbs left behind, and I'm done. I never feel trapped by the eating. It's not like a runaway train at all. It's more like a... a gentle stroll that I can end whenever I feel like I've walked far enough. I know some people probably struggle with that, where they just can't stop themselves once they start, but for me, the stopping is just as deliberate and controlled as the starting. I'm always the one in the driver's seat with it."
